title: Making a rejected number work: Charlie Cook's band
summary: With Charlie Cook's band a number was shelved until another band made it good; St. Cyr says the old bands worked on numbers until they worked.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, that they had. See, they, they, they, the fact that they were outlaw made them good. Because you'll find, I've experienced it with Charlie Cook's band. Charlie Cook has put numbers out for rehearsal. And the guys didn't like the number when they played it over the first time. And they made such a poor effort in playing the number that Charlie got disgusted and he put the number aside. He said, oh, we'll put this aside. Maybe later on we'll play it later. And maybe about three nights after, some guy come back and he'd come to work and I'd say, man, you remember that number we were playing the other day that you put back? Charlie Cook said, man, Horace Hyde played that number.
Man, you should, yeah, man, that number's good. You know what I mean? Well, those things.
Well, Charlie Hyde made the number good. See? The number was no better when Charlie Hyde got a lesser or-

The same number. They got the same time we did. But they worked on it and made something out of it, see? They might have changed the arrangement a little. They might have changed the rhythm. But it appealed to them when they heard it on the radio. But when he was trying to play it, it didn't appeal to them at all. They wouldn't even make a good effort to try to make something out of them. And that's the thing we used to do. We'd get a number and some of the guys would say, oh man, that's good. The hell ain't no good. They said, well, let's play it over. Let's make it good. Maybe the tempo's too slow or maybe it's too fast. Let's take the slow tempo and see what we can do with it, see? Well, they get to working on the numbers and some guy get an idea and, you know, he's injected into the numbers, you know, it's not on the music. But he gets out and thinks something sounds good and he turns loose with it. I said, well, that's good, man. Let's try it over again.
